Title: Beyond the “supply chain” framing: Cattle ranching as a vanishing mediator of deforestation and dispossession in the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon
Authors: Mairon G. Bastos Lima, Jesica López
Abstract: Unsustainable land-use change has become an increasingly critical social and environmental issue. Over a few decades, vast expanses of land with native vegetation or devoted to mixed-farming systems have given way to large-scale agriculture, incurring considerable biodiversity and livelihood loss. Cattle ranching and the production of a handful of internationally traded commodities such as soy and palm oil play a pivotal role in that expansion. They have led to numerous sustainability initiatives to curb their negative social and environmental impacts, yet a “supply chain” framing poses important limitations, for it typically fails to consider relationships between sectors and broader landscape dynamics. For one, there may be much stronger drivers than food consumption at play. This article draws from the frontier literature and explores the concept of “vanishing mediator” to analyze the role played by cattle ranching in particular. Comparing the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon, we assess how ranching intermediates an ongoing transition between pre-frontier forest areas and capital-intensive monocultures. We draw from land-use data and the scientific literature on each of the two cases as well as on a total of 30 key-informant interviews done in Brazil and Colombia. Our results show that cattle ranching’s role in spearheading deforestation in both countries cannot be understood without reference to its broader context, for it works as a vanishing mediator between pre-frontier settings and industrial agriculture. Ranching occupies frontiers with little infrastructure, paving the way for monocultures; it is instrumental to the land grabbing that makes the endeavor highly profitable; and, crucially, it precariously absorbs and co-opts displaced smallholders. Cattle ranching introduces the latter — as well as incoming settlers — to state institutions that previously neglected them and to a market-driven approach to land use that still preserves the trappings of rural living. Ultimately, however, people migrate to sprawling cities and clear the way for capital-intensive crops such as soy in Brazil and oil palm in Colombia. We conclude that the notion of individualized “supply chains” is shortsighted for dealing with such broader dynamics. Instead, effective sustainability interventions require addressing local vulnerabilities and investing in economic alternatives that can successfully hedge against deforestation drivers.

Title: Aid and armed actors: Collaboration and aid delivery in the DRC
Authors: Haley Swedlund, Marie-Eve Desrosiers, Joshua Fawcett Weiner, Pierre Sosthène Kambidi
Abstract: In conflict-affected contexts, the presence of armed actors—including state security forces, international peacekeeping missions, and non-state armed groups—means that aid organisations may need to cooperate with these actors to deliver foreign aid. Yet the conditions under which this cooperation happens remain underspecified. In this article, we use novel mixed methods data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to study these conditions. Building on qualitative interviews with Kinshasa-based aid practitioners, as well as a survey and survey experiment with Congolese provincial-level aid workers, we provide systematic evidence of the conditions under which humanitarian and development aid workers are more or less likely to collaborate with different types of armed actors across different regions of the country. We test three hypotheses: the type of armed actor, the visibility of cooperation, and the proximity to conflict. Our findings suggest that the type of armed actor and the proximity of the aid workers to conflict matter most. The public visibility of their collaboration is less important than anticipated. For those at the forefront of aid delivery, it is primarily the concrete realities and day-to-day interactions that appear to shape decision-making and behavior.

Title: Hydropower development, resettlement, and urban water security: Evidence from Brazil’s Belo Monte Dam
Authors: Heather Randell, Peter Taylor Klein, Thais Tartalha, Thaise Constancio Temoteo
Abstract: Millions of people are resettled each year when dam construction floods their homes and land. Dam building and its associated resettlement may impact water security by altering access to drinking water and sanitation, disrupting aquatic ecosystems, shifting local economies, and undermining the ability to use rivers for income, navigation, and cultural practices. This paper explores how dam-induced-displacement and resettlement in the Brazilian Amazon shaped women’s experiences of water (in)security along four dimensions: Access, Safety, Livelihoods, and Culture. We conducted in-depth interviews with 70 women in the city of Altamira who were impacted by the Belo Monte Dam and who had participated in household surveys before dam construction began. Our findings suggest that dam building and resettlement did not universally improve or degrade water security, but rather shifted it in uneven ways. While access to water improved for some women, the majority of respondents experienced water outages after the dam, some for weeks at a time. Safety from seasonal flooding and access to sanitation improved for many, though poor water quality and lack of maintenance of sanitation infrastructure created problems. Finally, resettlement and changes in river ecology undermined livelihoods for fisheries-dependent households and severed cultural connections to the river for many. These findings have crucial implications for health outcomes and can inform policies to improve the water security and well-being of populations resettled due to future dams, other development projects, and climate change.

Title: Corrigendum to “Development and interdisciplinarity: additional insights on the ‘economics silo’” [World Dev. 205(2026) 107435]
The development studies divide: fierce fault lines or fruitful frictions?
Abstract: The concept of development has deeply divided the social sciences concerned with peoples and earth's future. For many researchers and practitioners, variants of development are crucial normative cornerstones to frame and guide research and policy. Many critical scholars and activists associate the term with colonial, capitalist, extractivist, and patriarchal threats, and see it as the root cause of environmental degradation. In short, some study development as a solution, others as the problem. I call this rift the Development Studies Divide. After tracing diverse disciplinary roots, I discuss where the fault lines run and whether fruitful frictions could enrich the future of (critical) development studies. Despite stark differences in ideological, epistemological, and conceptual orientations, there is room for mutual learning, specifically across methodologies. A reflexive integration of critical perspectives with quantitative methods can substantiate critical claims beyond isolated case studies, address them at larger scales, and generate robust knowledge on alternatives to development beyond largely theory-driven proposals. It could also correct global empirical analyses that become problematic when their assumptions and interpretations are not grounded in the diverse histories, worldviews, and values of non-Western realities.

Title: Locus of control, climate change adaptation and perception: Evidence from rural Ethiopia
Authors: Halefom Yigzaw Nigus, Martin Paul Jr Tabe Ojong, Kibrom A. Abay
Abstract: Despite an overwhelming scientific consensus about the adverse effects of climate change and potential adaptation strategies, the uptake rates of climate adaptation practices fall short of expectations and public perceptions about the drivers and implications of climate change remain mixed. This paper examines whether farmers’ psychological traits, particularly locus of control, predict climate adaptation strategies. We focus on adoption of drought-tolerant varieties, fast-maturing varieties, early/late planting varieties, crop diversification, conservation agriculture, and water harvesting technologies using a large household survey from Ethiopia. We also explore climate change perceptions, and whether and how they align with actual climatic records. We find that farmers with a higher degree of internal locus of control are more likely to adopt various climate adaptation practices and are more likely to perceive changes in mean precipitation and temperature, while those with a higher level of external locus of control are less likely to perceive climate change and hence less likely to adopt climate-resilient practices. One standard deviation increase in internal (external) locus of control is associated with 3–5 percentage points higher (lower) probability of adopting alternative climate adaptation practices. We also find suggestive evidence that farmers’ climate adaptation responses are consistent with their climate perceptions and actual climatic records. These findings highlight the important role of behavioral attributes, including psychological traits, in explaining climate perceptions and subsequent climate actions.

Title: Why do eligible individuals fail to enrol for social assistance programmes? A systematic narrative review of factors affecting take-up
Abstract: Why do so many eligible individuals fail to sign up for government social assistance benefits? While non-take-up of social benefits is of great concern both for the effectiveness and equity of social policies, academics and policymakers continue to be puzzled by the lack of clarity on why people forgo increases in disposable income. Focusing on literature from the Global South, this review puts forward an analytical framework that identifies how structural conditions shape the context in which individual and institutional factors operate. Together, these interact to mitigate or exacerbate compliance, learning, and psychological costs as well as perceived relative benefits. Findings are synthesised around the three cost types. Overall, this review concludes that individual characteristics alone rarely explain non-take-up as their effects are moderated by the structural, programmatic and institutional conditions in which they operate. This helps explain why the literature often produces inconclusive or even contradictory findings regarding the determinants of take-up. These findings prompt further investigation into the structural conditions and programmatic and institutional factors that shape take-up gaps, and that policies aiming to close these gaps should consider.

Title: Heritage-sensitive interventions to support Indigenous peoples’ forest conservation: Evaluating an origin-label for highland produce in northern Thailand
Authors: Marco J. Haenssgen, Navaporn Sunanlikanon, Prasit Leepreecha, Mukdawan Sakboon, Putthida Kijdumnern, Giacomo Zanello, Daniele Asioli, Parichart Chawiwong, Pattarawadee Op-Ai, Inthanon Sutjathammawong, Phatsakorn Kiatsuntikun, Peter Petkoff, Anne Hertzog, Elizabeth Auclair, Ivo Vlaev
Abstract: Global conservation policies increasingly recognize the vital role of local and Indigenous communities in ecosystem protection, but mechanisms to support such communities’ livelihoods in a conservation context remain limited. Based on participatory engagement with diverse highland communities in the northern Thai tropics, we co-designed a highland origin label with the intention to alleviate Indigenous livelihood pressures. This study assessed whether this label can positively influence downstream urban consumers’ willingness-to-pay for Indigenous highland communities’ produce, using cross-sectional, qualitative, and choice experimental data. The study was implemented between February and April 2025 across four urban markets in Chiang Mai City, Thailand, including actual buying decisions for strawberries and chayote fruits and experimental exposure to background information on Indigenous highland livelihoods. The results from 888 real-market consumers revealed a substantial willingness-to-pay premium for origin-labelled products, with +11.6 Thai Baht/+56.3% on average (chayote: +10.4 Thai Baht/+50.0%; strawberries: +12.6 Thai Baht, +61.1%). Higher willingness-to-pay was positively associated with prior experience of purchasing labelled products and interest in Indigenous rights, negatively with price-conscious shoppers, and not associated with exposure to livelihood information. Large classes of shoppers (at least 75.9%) exhibited high utility for the origin label. Qualitative responses indicated strong positive sentiment and label credibility, although with a risk of overinterpretation. We conclude that co-developed origin labels can elicit substantial consumer willingness-to-pay, but translating it into tangible support for Indigenous livelihoods would require further considerations of agricultural value chain optimisation, cooperative support, channels for direct and consumer-segment-specific marketing, and tackling problematic Indigenous stereotypes.

Title: Sowing discontent: Foreign land acquisitions and satisfaction with democracy in Africa
Abstract: Foreign direct investment (FDI) in agriculture—particularly through large-scale land acquisitions—has become increasingly common across Africa. While existing studies have focused on the economic and environmental implications of these investments, their political effects remain underexplored. This study investigates how foreign land acquisitions shape citizens’ satisfaction with democracy in African democracies. By integrating spatial data from the Land Matrix with geo-referenced Afrobarometer survey responses (2002–2018), this study employs a difference-in-differences design to identify the causal impact of proximity to operational land deals. The findings suggest that foreign land acquisitions reduce democratic satisfaction through instrumental and intrinsic pathways. However, when local communities are meaningfully consulted, these negative effects are significantly mitigated. The results underscore that substantive consultation with local communities is a prerequisite for aligning foreign investment with sustainable development and inclusive growth, thereby offering new insights into how land-based FDI shapes democratic legitimacy in developing countries.

Title: How do common pool natural resources relate to rural income, poverty and inequality? A multi-country assessment
Authors: Anamika Das, Sharachchandra Lele, Brian Robinson, Geoff Wells, Suman Attiwilli, Mahesh Poudyal, Kate S. chreckenberg, Tim Daw, Siddappa Setty
Abstract: The role of Common Pool natural Resources (CPRs) such as forests, grasslands, rivers, lakes, wetlands and oceans in rural economies has been much debated in the literature, often on the basis of micro-level or provincial-scale analyses and focusing on a single type of CPR, typically forests. This study draws on data from 6,509 households across fifteen regions in nine low and middle-income countries covering Africa, Asia, and Latin America that also cover a diverse set of CPRs, including forests, savannas, grasslands, mangroves and inland and marine fisheries. We estimate the contribution of CPR-based income to total household income and vis-a-vis the poverty line across income classes, and analyse the correlates of CPR-based income and the relationship between CPR income and income inequality within rural settlements. Our results highlight three important aspects of the CPR-rural income relationship. First, they confirm that CPR-based income makes up a significant portion of the income of the rural poor even across diverse geographies and CPRs. Households below the World Bank $1.9 per capita per day poverty line derive on average one fourth of their household income from CPRs. Second, the regression results highlight the importance of physical resource abundance and social accessibility, household demography, the regional demographic/market context, and most importantly the complementary productive assets owned by households in deriving income from CPRs. Third, there is a distinct correlation between the broad nature of CPR harvest technologies and income-inequality: when the harvest technology is capital-intensive, richer households derive more monetary benefit from CPRs, not only in absolute terms but also in terms of share in household income, leading to a situation where such CPRs exacerbate inequality within settlements. Our results highlight the importance of integrating a diversity of CPRs and CPR availability, access and technological context into CPR studies. They also highlight the need for pro-poor policies that go beyond securing resource access and include support for the poor to access technologies and markets.

Title: The politics of climate adaptation in Nepal: authority, knowledge, and resource inequality in multi-level governance
Abstract: Contemporary approaches to climate change adaptation increasingly emphasize multi-level stakeholder engagement. These approaches seek to advance sustainability, equity, and inclusion while addressing the social, environmental, economic, and political needs of present and future generations. Although technocratic adaptation addresses biophysical climate risks, it often neglects socio-political forces that shape vulnerability and can intensify long-term climate risks and inequalities. This paper utilizes a multi-level governance framework to examine the political dimensions of climate adaptation, focusing on the dynamics of authority, knowledge, and resource access. Building on literature on the political dimensions of climate change adaptation, this study draws on ethnographic data to examine how power is exercised, negotiated, and resisted across multiple governance scales in Nepal. Focusing on the Karnali region, it shows that despite formally democratic multi-level institutions, adaptation authority remains centralized at the federal level and shaped by corruption, reinforcing exclusion and elite capture. As federal, provincial, and local governments compete over authority, knowledge production, and resource control, Nepal's multi-level adaptation governance reinforces power differentials and elite influence while marginalizing vulnerable communities, thereby limiting transformative and just climate adaptation. This paper argues that effective adaptation requires accountable multi-level governance rather than decentralization alone. Meaningful subnational authority must be matched by cross-scale coordination, transparency, and oversight so that decision-making, resources, and knowledge are not captured by elites at any level.

Title: The gender dimension of refugees’ integration in the labor market
Authors: Tobias Müller, Pia Pannatier, Martina Viarengo
Abstract: This paper examines the gender differences in labor market integration among refugees and their determinants. It focuses on a longitudinal dataset that covers the entire refugee population in Switzerland over 20 years. During the period examined, the majority of refugees came from low-income economies in Africa and Asia. The quasi-random allocation of asylum seekers across Swiss cantons, which differ in their socio-economic characteristics, provides a natural experiment to identify the effects of source country culture and the role of local initial conditions in shaping refugees’ labor-market integration trajectories. Our empirical findings show that women refugees from countries with more conservative gender norms (measured by female-to-male labor force participation ratios and fertility rates) have less favorable labor market outcomes, with these effects varying in their persistence over time. The analysis further reveals the negative role of initial unemployment and the positive role of co-ethnic networks in the cantons of arrival, with these effects varying by gender and network characteristics. Finally, local attitudes toward gender equality reduce the gender gap in labor market outcomes among refugees.

Title: Rentier resource nationalism and overseas investment by multinational corporations: the impact of resource value
Abstract: Characterized by its predatory nature and the institutional uncertainty, rentier resource nationalism (RRN) has emerged as a critical risk factor for overseas investment by multinational corporations (MNCs). However, existing literature rarely relies on theoretical models to analyze the differential impacts of RRN across heterogeneous investment objectives. Furthermore, the underlying role of resource value remains underexplored, particularly from the perspective of “cognitive divergence”. To address these gaps, this study develops a three-stage game model and investigates how RRN and resource value affect the economic variables of MNCs. The results reveal that RRN significantly reduces the residual profit and overseas investment outlay of MNCs, while increasing metal output. Through the lens of investment objective heterogeneity, MNCs targeting residual profit maximization suffer negative shocks. Conversely, MNCs aiming to ensure more resource supply can benefit from the dynamics, and exhibit a higher tolerance threshold for RRN intensity. The ultimate impact of resource value hinges on the relative strength of the market-size driving effect versus the resource-depletion inhibitory effect. Crucially, “cognitive divergence” regarding resource value serves as an important mechanism explaining the simultaneous emergence of intensified RRN and the expansion of investment outlay. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the rational formulation of RRN policies and enriches the theoretical framework of international investment.

Title: Scarred by nature: How early exposure to natural disasters shapes risk attitudes
Abstract: Can early-life experiences shape long-term risk attitudes? This paper examines the relationship between exposure to natural disasters during early adulthood and individual risk preferences later in life. Using harmonized survey data linked to disaster records, we find that individuals exposed to natural disasters between the ages of 18 and 25 exhibit significantly greater risk aversion later in life. This relationship proves robust across a range of alternative specifications. We further explore the role of cultural transmission as a mechanism, showing that social connectedness moderates the observed behavioral shift. Our findings underscore the impressionable years as a critical window for the formation of individual preferences. The study offers new insights into how climate-related shocks are linked to long-lasting behavioral patterns, with implications for public policy, economic behavior, and climate adaptation.

Title: Cash transfers and time use within the household: an analysis of the effect of Familias en Acción
Authors: Edgar Marcillo-Yepez, Maira Emy Reimão, Conner Mullally, Pilar Useche
Abstract: Conditional cash transfers (CCTs) have been found to have several benefits, particularly with respect to educational outcomes of targeted children. However, concerns have also been raised that CCTs may further push women into traditional gender norms, as they make mothers responsible for ensuring that their children meet the conditionalities and that their family receives the transfer. We analyze 2020–21 time use data from Colombia, and find that the CCT Familias en Acción increased the time that mothers allocated to domestic work, particularly when they have children aged 6–14. This pattern does not come from a substitution between children's and mothers’ domestic labor, but, rather, reveals that the cash transfer enabled women to decrease their labor force participation during the pandemic – but that their time was then reallocated toward more domestic work, following traditional norms.

Title: Editorial Board
Identifying the types of government interventions that work in the sanitation sector
Authors: Britta Augsburg, Habiba Djebbari, Molly Lipscomb, Tetsushi Sonobe

Title: Development approaches for preventing violent extremism: A systematic review of the empirical evidence
Authors: Leanne M. Kelly, Greg Barton, Anthony Ware
Abstract: This systematic review examines English-language publications documenting primary-level community programming for preventing and countering violent extremism (P/CVE) undertaken by development civil society and non-government organisations (CSO/NGOs). The objective is to identify and critically analyse the strengths, problems, gaps, and opportunities in incorporating P/CVE into international and community development work. This focus is necessary because primary-level interventions target broad community resilience, unlike secondary and tertiary interventions, which focus on at-risk or radicalised individuals. Given that development CSOs working on P/CVE programs operate independently from government-led counterterrorism efforts, this review provides insights specific to non-securitised, community-level, development-driven approaches. Source inclusion parameters were set to require empirical studies on primary-level P/CVE programs run by development CSOs. Studies of secondary and tertiary interventions, government-led programs, and initiatives by educational or religious institutions were excluded to maintain the focus on non-state, community-level, development-driven approaches. There was no restriction on location, publication date, or publication type, with both peer-reviewed and grey-literature publications included. As the P/CVE field is relatively new, it was expected that the search would mostly find publications from the 2010s and 2020s, which proved to be the case, with the earliest publication being from 2008. Records were identified using Google Scholar, Google, JSTOR Security Studies, 3ie, ALNAP, OECD iLibrary, and institutional websites, with a final search occurring on 31 January 2024. Bias was assessed by recording authors’ affiliation with the evaluand (although internal evaluations were not excluded on that basis). Extracted data was analysed using grounded theory to inductively determine themes. The systematic review incorporates 129 studies reported in 137 papers: 64% qualitative, 32% mixed-methods, and 4% quantitative. Of these, 53% were industry and evaluation reports, 31% articles, 10% books/chapters, and 6% theses. Limitations include the heterogeneity of included studies and limited evaluation rigour, which constrain reliable conclusions of program effectiveness in many papers. Grounded analysis identified three overarching thematic groupings: interconnections, power and relations, and impact. Common findings across papers highlighted the opportunities for P/CVE programming to enhance the work already being conducted by development CSOs, although papers cautioned that this needs to be carefully designed, implemented, and assessed with consideration of context, objectives, appropriate terminology, local agency, sustainability, marginalised groups, and potential for perverse outcomes. The need for consistent, long-term, untied funding of development CSOs’ P/CVE programs was frequently raised, as was the importance of prioritising local participation in all aspects of programming. Many papers noted the value of effective coordination and collaboration horizontally between communities and CSOs as well as vertically between global and local authorities and academia. Evidence of effectiveness was heterogeneous, with some studies measuring impact and others measuring satisfaction. This likely underlies a particular problem with monitoring and evaluation in this nascent field rather than necessarily representing problematic programming. Key issues with monitoring and evaluation typically include unclear and infeasible theories of change, poor monitoring practices, and limited ability to conduct rigorous evaluation due to insufficient funding and capacity. The most promising practices centred on the evaluation of changes in knowledge, attitudes, social cohesion, and wellbeing. Rather than trying to evaluate the impact of a development program on a reduction in violent extremism, these evaluations demonstrated how

Title: When cash enters local markets: local economic spillover effects of cash transfers, remittances, and insurance
Abstract: Insurance payouts, remittances, and government cash transfers all share one feature: they inject cash into local markets. While these interventions typically aim to improve the welfare of recipients, they can also affect the economic welfare of non-recipients. Yet our understanding of such economic spillover effects remains limited. Empirical studies report mixed findings, ranging from welfare-increasing to welfare-decreasing spillover effects, while the theoretical literature discussing potential mechanisms remains fragmented and lacks an integrated framework. This study develops a structured conceptual synthesis that integrates dispersed theoretical and empirical insights on the spillover effects of cash injections. We first develop a unified theoretical framework identifying the key mechanisms and moderating factors shaping spillovers, and then review the empirical literature through its lens. The framework highlights that spillover effects emerge through changes in local prices, wages, and resource sharing within social networks. We further show that the magnitude and direction of these effects depend on the interaction between cash-injection-specific parameters and the local environment, including its local economic structure and the constraints that recipient and non-recipient households face. By integrating insights across studies on cash transfers, remittances, and insurance programs, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for understanding spillover patterns of cash injections more broadly. Our analysis generates policy-relevant insights and highlights several important gaps in the current literature.

Title: Can policy design build trust in local taxation? Experimental evidence of property taxation in Mexican municipalities
Abstract: Property taxes, the primary source of local revenue for municipal governments, are essential for improving urban service provision and resident welfare. Yet this tax is widely unpopular and often politically contentiuous. This study's descriptive findings reveal that property owners are not currently motivated to pay their property taxes by the promise of collective benefits, but rather by the desire to secure their property rights. Thus, this study asks: What dimensions of property tax design do property owners prioritize? How do they negotiate trade-offs? And can policy design establish credible commitment? I address these questions using an experimental conjoint survey with over 2,000 property owners in 34 urban municipalities in Mexico. I find that property owners are largely indifferent to the progressivity of property tax increases yet strongly prioritize policies that enhance accountability in how government administers, spends, and enforces taxes. Specifically, the presence of active oversight strategies in the use of funds increases the support for a policy by 11 percentage points, an effect greater than that of policies that offer more direct benefits. Individuals with high perceptions of government corruption disproportionately favor tax policies that incorporate active transparency strategies even if this implies a higher fiscal burden. Overall, this study demonstrates that public support for property taxation is not entirely inelastic and that adopting accountability measures that signal how funds are spent can make property owners more accepting of tax increases. This study contributes to literature on the fiscal contract by demonstrating how policy designs that enhance accountability can help establish credible commitment.

Title: Partisan politics and sectoral policy in Africa’s agro-export commodity chains
Abstract: Even after economic liberalization in the 1990s, the role of the state in Africa's traditional tropical commodity export sectors has remained extensive. This paper argues that post-liberalization, these patterns of state regulation have often been shaped by the pressures and incentives of partisan politics, just as they were in earlier decades. We compare and contrast the changing institutional structure and patterns of state regulation in four agricultural commodity export sectors: Côte d'Ivoire-cocoa, Ghana-cocoa, Kenya-coffee, and Uganda-coffee. In spite of important differences, all four sectors are critical in providing resources, organizational structure, and policy mechanisms for building and maintaining electoral and other forms of political support for historically powerful political parties and/or power contenders. Post-1990s, each of the four cases presents an alternative pattern of alignment between export-sector organizations and partisan politics. Comparison across cases reveals the depth and variety of the ways in which domestic politics in African countries, including electoral politics, can shape state intervention in commodity chains for agro-exports, even in the neoliberal era. One implication for development studies is that domestic political and partisan dynamics are likely to continue to influence how governments use their “policy space” in supply chain governance in the future.

Title: Migration opportunities and human capital investments
Abstract: We examine how shocks to migration opportunities affect schooling outcomes in origin communities. We focus on the migration between Mexico and the United States, and exploit the expansion of the Secure Communities program in the US—a federal data-sharing program that substantially increased the risk of deportation for illegal migrants—as an exogenous shock to the attractiveness of illegal migration. Our results suggest that the Secure Communities program increased attendance, enrollment, and educational attainment in municipalities that had stronger migration-network links with counties in the US that adopted the program early-on relative to municipalities that had ties with US counties that introduced the policy somewhat later. These results are consistent with the interpretation that the Secure Communities program raised the returns to education for prospective migrants by making low-skill migration to the US less attractive.

Title: Is irregular migration responsive to recent German asylum policy adjustments?
Authors: Bernd Beber, Cara Ebert, Maximiliane Sievert
Abstract: We investigate the extent to which asylum policies that aim to deter individuals from migrating irregularly in fact do so. We specifically consider effects of Germany’s 2023 asylum policy adjustments, which include accelerated asylum decision processes, the prospect of asylum processing outside of Europe, the introduction of a payment card to replace cash benefits, and an extended waiting period for native-level benefits. To estimate the effects of these policy measures on irregular migration intent, we implement a conjoint experiment with 989 men aged 18–40 in four cities in Senegal, a country where irregular migration to Europe is highly salient. Offshoring the asylum process substantially lowers irregular migration intentions, and extending the waiting time for native-level benefits only has a small effect on intent. Neither reducing asylum processing times nor replacing cash benefits with a payment card alters intentions. Our study does not resolve political and normative questions concerning these policies.

Title: The contributions of community forests to rural prosperity in the United States
Authors: Reem Hajjar, Susan Charnley, Gregory E. Frey, Kathleen McGinley, John Schelhas, Frederick W. Cubbage
Abstract: Community forests (CFs) are a forest ownership and governance approach that enable community members and other key stakeholders to cooperatively manage local forests to produce a range of benefits that align with local community priorities. While well-studied internationally, there is a lack of research that systematically documents how CFs can contribute to rural prosperity in the U.S. amidst ongoing socioeconomic and environmental change. We adapt a framework developed to characterize the contributions of forests to rural prosperity in the international context to investigate the environmental, economic, and social benefits from CFs. In examining 18 in-depth CF case studies, we find that establishing CFs increases access to and control over local forests by local communities, allowing them to manage forests according to local priorities and needs. Economically, many CFs bring in earned income and employment, directly and indirectly, from forest products and services, and support local businesses through tourism and recreation. Social benefits of CFs include access to recreation opportunities, enhancing social relations, and building community identity, security, and empowerment. In extending existing rural prosperity frameworks, we propose that environmental benefits of CFs, including forest protection and restoration and reducing wildfire risk, also play a key role in enhancing rural prosperity. Evidence from these cases suggests that local governance of forests for the production of local benefits using a CF model is a promising approach to enhancing rural prosperity in the U.S.

Title: Revolutionizing the underworld: Can the digital economy shrink the informal economy?
Authors: Zhike Lv, Wenqing Dai, Lei Han, Lingling Jiang
Abstract: The informal economy has come under increasing scrutiny. Rather than relying on coercive measures, efforts should focus on formalizing the informal economy by expanding the formal sector, with the digital economy playing a pivotal role in this transition. This study examines the influence of the digital economy on the informal economy across 89 countries from 2003 to 2017, using a two-way fixed effects regression method. The study draws the following conclusions. Firstly, the digital economy contributes to a significant reduction in the size of the informal economy, a result supported by robustness tests. Secondly, the mechanism test results reveal that this reduction is driven by improvements in institutional quality and financial inclusion. Finally, the heterogeneity test suggests that the influence of the digital economy is particularly strong in countries with higher levels of economic development and educational attainment. Overall, these findings complement existing studies, deliver helpful implications for policymakers, and suggest some new lines for future research.

Title: Growing global shipping costs increase population mortality in Africa
Abstract: Reducing mortality is vital for Africa, whose economy depends on global shipping. This paper provides novel insights into the effects of global shipping costs on population mortality, which has been largely overlooked. For the first time, we investigated the relationship between shipping costs and population mortality across 45 African countries from 2000 to 2020. We found that the rising dry bulk shipping cost was significantly associated with higher population mortality, particularly among women in African countries, which were net importers of dry bulk commodities. It was revealed that East Africa was more vulnerable to shipping cost shocks than West Africa. Furthermore, by integrating climate factors with a long short-term memory model, we predicted the trends in shipping costs for 2040, 2070, and 2100 under different climate change scenarios and investigated the potential threats these changes pose to population mortality in Africa. The results show that population mortality in Africa is likely to face increasing challenges due to the rise in shipping costs under future climate change scenarios and global disruptions such as pandemics and financial crises. The population mortality in Africa may reach 10.06143 - 12.1939 deaths per 1,000 people, with total deaths ranging from 15.90 to 31.36 million. These findings provide new insights into the potential benefits of reducing global shipping costs for improving health outcomes in Africa.

Title: Refugees, camps, and host communities: Evidence from Bangladesh’s humanitarian hosting system
Authors: Alvin Etang Ndip, Sandra V. Rozo, María José Urbina, Christina Wieser
Abstract: By 2025, over 42 million refugees will be hosted in low- and middle-income countries, which rely on one of two models: a humanitarian model centered on international aid and camp-based restrictions on integration, or a development-based model promoting self-reliance and gradual integration. We study the local development impacts of a pure humanitarian model, focusing on Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. Combining remote sensing data with longitudinal household surveys, we exploit variation in distance to refugee camps before and after the refugee influx to explore the effects of this refugee hosting model. We find that areas closer to camps experienced higher economic growth following the arrival of the Rohingya. Household-level evidence points to humanitarian aid as the key mechanism: host communities near camps exhibit higher job formality, aid access, and food consumption. However, proximity to camps is also associated with adverse effects, including increased safety concerns and a higher prevalence of communicable diseases among host populations. These results are consistent with epidemiological spillovers and increased pressure on local infrastructure offsetting gains from expanded service provision.

Title: Distance, prospects, and migration to towns and cities
Authors: Joachim De Weerdt, Luc Christiaensen, Ravi Kanbur
Abstract: This study examines the relative importance of distance and urban prospects in migrants’ destination choice and explores its implications for understanding migration patterns across towns and cities. It uses an exceptional 18-year panel of individuals migrating from the rural and remote Kagera region of Tanzania, complemented with information on the possible destinations from the Tanzanian census. Applying dyadic regressions and controlling for individual heterogeneity, it finds that destinations farther away or with lower prospects are less likely, consistent with the literature. Education makes distance less important, and poverty at origin more. Simulations based on the estimated coefficients help explain why far more migrants from Kagera end up in towns than cities: towns are sufficiently closer to the rural poor so that their advantages of proximity outweigh their lower prospects relative to cities. Given that about two-thirds of the rural population in low-income countries live within two hours from a town, many of them poor or with little formal education, these findings open a broader discussion on the role of towns in fostering development and poverty reduction.

Title: No man’s land? The effect of forced displacement on forest cover change in Colombia
Abstract: Globally, state-based armed conflict has increased by more than 50 percent over the past decade. The environmental consequences of such conflict are often overlooked. To help fill that gap, we examine the effect on forest cover of conflict-related forced displacement in Colombia. We use fine-scale annual data on forest cover change derived from satellite images along with data culled from court records of displacement events, using computational text analysis, to estimate staggered difference-in-differences models. We find that displacement leads to a 50 percent increase in deforestation. This effect is likely due to the expansion of both legal and illegal economic activities following displacement. It is most pronounced when paramilitary groups are the sole actors involved in displacement and where economic returns to cleared land uses are high. In principle, these results could be used to target efforts to reduce environmental damage associated with civil conflict.

Title: Corrigendum to “No need to wait for reporting – Examining learning from results-based management practices in development cooperation” [World Dev. 206 (2026) 107451]
Authors: Janet Vähämäki, Annika Hilgert, Kathrin Wolf, Martin Bruder
Abstract: The authors regret, that we misunderstood the revision process and specifically when and where we were supposed to fill in the double affiliation. I/Janet Vähämäki am employed both at the Stockholm School of Economics and Stockholm Environment Institute and have worked with the project at both institutions. However, only SSE has an Open Access agreement with Elsevier and their conditions for approving the Open Access fee from their side is that I insert them as the main affiliation for this article. Title: Employment aspirations of young agroindustry workers in Peru – Poverty, gender and role models
Abstract: Aspirations are a key dimension of wellbeing but remain underexplored among agrifood system workers. This study examines the employment aspirations of 528 young individuals in Peru who intended to work in the horticultural agro-industry, using two-round panel survey data and econometric methods. Between survey rounds, 414 respondents entered employment for the first time, allowing us to analyze how early labor market experiences shape aspirations related to income, occupation, and promotion. We assess how aspirations are influenced by gender, poverty status, and the presence of workplace role models. The findings show that agro-industry jobs can raise aspirations and help reduce gender- and poverty-related gaps. Supervisors—especially those who are female and age-proximate—play a significant role in shaping youth aspirations, particularly for women. The study highlights the potential of targeted employment strategies, such as thoughtful supervisor-worker matching as practical tools to promote more equitable labor outcomes and foster upward mobility among rural youth.

Title: Coups d’état and the informal economy
Authors: Ablam Estel Apeti, Dorgyles C.M. Kouakou, Assi Okara, Kolotioloma I.H. Yéo
Abstract: This paper analyzes the effect of coups d’état on the size of the informal economy in a large sample of 98 developing countries observed over the period 1993–2020. Using a matched difference-in-differences approach that combines a two-way fixed effects model with entropy balancing, we find that the occurrence of a coup d’état significantly increases the size of the informal economy. This result is robust across a variety of tests, including event-study analysis, propensity score matching, treatment effect methods based on inverse probability weighting, generalized method of moments estimation, fixed-effects regressions, a falsification test, checks for potential omitted variables, alternative data sources for coups d’état, the exclusion of nonmilitary coups, and accounting for coup d’état spillover effects. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the detrimental effect of coups d’état holds for both successful and failed coups and is influenced by structural factors. Specifically, the effect decreases with higher levels of domestic credit to the private sector, remittances, quality of regulation, and net official development assistance received. Conversely, the effect increases with higher real GDP per capita, democracy, unemployment, oil rents, and income inequality. Higher external debt, lower gross fixed capital formation, and erosion of democracy are the main channels through which coups d’état expand the informal economy in developing countries.

Title: Beyond the aid model: innovating university-community partnerships in remote rural China
Authors: Xun Li, Luan Chen, Ye Long, Xianyu Hou, Jin Wang
Abstract: Why do so many well-intentioned aid programs in remote areas fail to bring durable outcomes? A common explanation attributes failure to local communities’ lack of knowledge or capacity. This paper argues instead that dependency is embedded in the one-directional structure of aid itself. As an alternative, it introduces a university-community co-practice model that fosters two-way collaboration and integrates external resources into villagers’ everyday practices, through which cognitive, relational, and structural forms of social capital are generated. Drawing on more than five years of action research in two villages in southwestern China, the study shows how universities and villagers collaborated in a paired assistance program to renovate houses and courtyards through hands-on co-practice and mutual learning. These small-scale interventions not only improved living conditions but also enabled villagers to maintain and adapt the initiatives after external experts withdrew. The findings suggest that the university-community partnerships can transform short-term aid into more equitable and resilient rural development by embedding development processes in locally grounded networks of social capital.

Title: Bridging the gap: how renewable energy development reduces urban-rural income inequality in China
Authors: Jing-Yue Liu, Quan Lei, Yue-Jun Zhang
Abstract: Renewable energy development is central to climate change mitigation, but whether it also reduces urban–rural income inequality remains unclear. Using panel data for 271 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2005 to 2019, we combine two-way fixed-effects models with an instrumental-variable strategy to estimate the effect of renewable energy development on the urban–rural income gap. The results show that renewable energy development significantly reduces urban–rural income inequality: a one-standard-deviation increase lowers the gap by about 11%, and this finding remains robust across multiple robustness checks. The effect is more evident in regions with richer solar resources, lower fossil energy dependence, and lower urbanization levels. Mechanism analyses further suggest that this effect operates by improving rural employment and enhancing educational accessibility in rural areas. We also find that the inequality-reducing effect is significantly strengthened in regions with more developed green finance, highlighting the enabling role of green finance in renewable expansion. These findings show that renewable energy development can generate both climate and equity gains, with important implications for coordinated urban–rural development. We therefore recommend prioritizing renewable projects in rural areas with strong resource endowments and lower urbanization levels, while strengthening green finance systems to support more inclusive development.

Title: The spatial allocation effects of central transfers: evidence from China
Abstract: Coordinating the fiscal relations between the central and local governments is a worldwide governance challenge. Based on a spatial general equilibrium framework, we quantify the aggregate effects of tax-sharing adjustments (i.e. fiscal revenue division) and the spatial allocation of central transfers (i.e. fiscal expenditure assignment) through labor migration. Calibrating the model for China, we find that adjusting the tax-sharing ratio induces co-directional changes in regional disparity, aggregate output, and welfare. Changes in the spatial allocation structure of central transfers during 2016–2021 mitigated labor misallocation, reducing regional disparities by 1.09% and increasing aggregate output by 4.44%, but causing welfare to decline by 3.03%. A reduction in labor migration costs amplifies the spatial allocation effects of central transfers. Moreover, the spatial allocation effects of different types of central transfers show significant differences.

Title: Too complex to collaborate? Rethinking CSO–municipal relations for public service provision
Abstract: Collaboration between civil society organizations (CSOs) and municipalities is often seen as beneficial for service delivery, especially in under-resourced cities where local governments face capacity and operational constraints. However, it remains unclear how these partnerships influence performance across services of differing complexity. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork in Peruvian municipalities, this article examines how collaboration with community-based CSOs affects outcomes in simple versus complex services, using waste management as a comparative case. The analysis focuses on three proximate relational mechanisms: municipal collaboration management capacity, local officials’ perceptions of CSOs, and CSO leadership engagement. The findings show that these factors interact to shape service performance, with their impact conditioned by service complexity. While collaboration can succeed under suboptimal conditions in simple services, complex services perform well where the three elements are jointly strong and aligned. The study highlights the need to strengthen collaboration management, challenge municipal biases, and support CSO leadership—particularly in settings facing complex service challenges.

Title: The unexpected role of conditionality in shaping relational values: Insights from an incentive-based conservation program in Bolivia
Authors: Brooke McWherter, Will Munger, Zhao Ma, Claudia Radel, Laura Zanotti, Jonathan Bauchet, Ricardo Godoy
Abstract: As global change accelerates, Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) programs have become increasingly important tools for addressing the interconnected challenges of land degradation, biodiversity loss, water scarcity, and climate change. PES programs provide incentives to individuals or communities, conditional on people adopting sustainable natural resource management practices to support or increase ecosystem service provisioning. Although conditionality is considered a “PES-defining feature,” little is known about how conditionality is perceived by community members and how such perceptions influence their participation in and experience with PES programs. To address this gap, we conducted an extensive qualitative study of Watershared, a Bolivian PES program, to investigate (1) how community members perceive conditionality in PES and its two components—monitoring and sanction, and (2) how removing conditionality influences PES participants’ perceptions of the program and relationship with the implementing organization. We found that Watershared participants perceived monitoring as more than just a compliance check mechanism; they saw it as a form of technical support and relationship building, which strengthens their relational values toward both nature and the program itself. Participants were generally unconcerned about sanctioning, with many viewing sanctioning as unnecessary or unenforceable, despite the implementing organization having imposed sanctions previously. Watershared participants with unconditional contracts generally noticed the removal of conditionality, with some interpreting it as a lack of care and reciprocity from the implementing organization. These results highlight how relational values were developed and supported through the two components of conditionality in PES. These results suggest that the role of conditionality in PES may be less about surveillance and penalty to ensure conservation, but more about serving as an avenue to activate and strengthen community members’ relational values toward nature and the PES-implementing organization, which may, in turn, improve program effectiveness and future participation. In the face of intensifying global environmental change, such relational values tied to conditionality in PES, as identified in this research, are critical for fostering and sustaining cooperation, trust, and long-term commitment to conservation.

Title: Beyond urban–rural divides: A distributional analysis of spatial inequality in the WAEMU
Abstract: This study re-examines spatial inequality in the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) by moving beyond the conventional urban–rural dichotomy and introducing a classification that distinguishes leading and lagging regions within both urban and rural areas. I quantify the contribution of these spatial divides to overall welfare inequality using harmonized household survey data and assess whether spatial gaps reflect differences in endowments or in the returns to those endowments. Combining Theil index decomposition with recentered influence function (RIF) regressions, I show that leading–lagging disparities account for a substantial share of total inequality, frequently exceeding the standard urban–rural divide's contribution. The differences in returns are particularly pronounced toward the upper end of the welfare distribution, indicating that similar assets yield systematically uneven outcomes across space. These findings show that spatial inequality in WAEMU reflects not only unequal asset distribution but also structurally differentiated returns. Therefore, policies aimed at reducing regional disparities must address access to productive resources and the institutional and market environments shaping their returns. More broadly, this study illustrates how harmonized household surveys combined with distribution-sensitive decomposition methods can uncover the structural dimensions of spatial inequality in developing economies.

Title: Hospital allocation and politicians: Evidence from Malaysia
Abstract: Equitable access to healthcare requires efficient allocation of health infrastructure, yet politics may distort these decisions. This paper studies how politicians distort public hospital allocations in postcolonial Malaysia from 1959 to 2013. Malaysia first allocates hospital funding to districts, then selects specific locations within funded districts for construction. Using six decades of data on hospital construction and elections, I find that constituencies represented by deputy ministers are significantly more likely to receive new hospitals, but only at the location selection stage within districts. District-level funding decisions effectively direct resources to districts far from existing hospitals. I provide suggestive evidence that measurable guidelines for funding decisions exist but not for construction site selection. These results suggest that defining clear guidelines in hospital allocation can limit political distortions.

Title: The politician, the press and the public: How politicians’ perceptions of the media shape UK aid allocations
Abstract: This paper examines politicians’ attitudes and beliefs about the press, their potential role in shaping aid policy and how these views differ from the public’s. We address these questions using survey data from 107 UK MPs and 2047 members of the UK public. We find a positive association between MPs’ beliefs that the news media influence public opinion, reflect public opinion, and are central to a political career—and a belief that the news media should influence aid policy. This suggests that politicians’ attitudes and beliefs about the media can play a role in shaping aid policy. We also find that MPs are significantly more likely to think that the media influences public attitudes towards aid spending than the public. This suggests that politicians could potentially be overweighing news coverage when making decisions about aid spending. Overall, these findings help fill an important gap in our understanding of what happens ‘upstream’ of aid allocations and add further nuance to our understanding of the media’s political effects.

Title: Mobile money and the social contract: Experimental evidence from Ghana
Abstract: Mobile money platforms are ubiquitous in many emerging economies. Hailed for raising financial inclusion and economic wellbeing, governments have now turned to mobile payments as a source of tax revenue. Transaction levies are often regressive, unpopular, and can encourage a return to cash. We present experimental evidence that they may also harm tax morale, a core component of the social contract between citizen and state. We present results from a survey experiment in Ghana, in which priming a controversial mobile transaction levy significantly lowers support for the state’s right to collect taxes and willingness to comply with tax laws. We combine this with focus group discussions and analyse effect heterogeneity to examine two pre-registered explanations: transaction taxes cost citizens more than they expect to gain (reciprocity) and provoke particular backlash from non-government voters (partisanship). Our findings suggest that taxing mobile money can undermine efforts to expand fiscal capacity, while raising important mechanistic and policy questions for future research.

Title: Enforcing discipline in China: Countering internal misinformation with public disclosure
Authors: Handi Li, Shengqiao Lin, Minh D. Trinh
Abstract: Governments around the world need internal discipline to ensure the implementation of policies and delivery of governance outputs, and this need is more severe in authoritarian systems that govern top-down and without bottom-up electoral pressures. Conventional wisdom suggests that autocrats rely on punishment to discipline subordinates who fail to obey orders, but we argue that public disclosure of such malfeasance can also be effective, even when unaccompanied by punishment. In the case of internal misinformation—the tampering of government data and statistics by local agents to distort central authorities’ decisions—we find that the Chinese government successfully adopted public disclosure to combat the manipulation of local GDP numbers by lower-level governments. Our evidence indicates that publicly disclosing a prior act of falsification reduced future manipulation and did so at various levels of local governments, even as officials implicated by the disclosure faced no career setbacks. Hinting at downstream impacts, such disclosure also improved confidence among economic actors, evidenced by increased business activity in localities involved in public disclosures.

Title: Full-day school programs and higher education: Evidence from Peru
Authors: Vania Bitia Salas García, Germán Vega Acuña, Stefani Seminario Solano, Sinthia Morales Mendoza
Abstract: Full-day school programs aim to promote development by improving students’ learning outcomes. We estimate the impact of Peru's full-day secondary school reform, Jornada Escolar Completa (JEC), on higher education attainment. Using data from the Young Lives Study, we construct a grouped-sibling sample linking younger siblings who could attend JEC secondary schools with their older siblings who did not attend. The identification strategy relies on within-household variation and a difference-in-differences framework comparing changes in higher education attainment between households affected and not affected by the JEC program. We find that JEC increases the likelihood of pursuing higher education, with effects concentrated in technical rather than university studies. Our findings also suggest larger gains among students from disadvantaged backgrounds, pointing to the potential of JEC to narrow inequalities in access to higher education. Time-use data show that JEC students remain engaged in learning, with no increase in absenteeism or decline in study time at home. Rather, they compensate for longer school days by cutting back on leisure and work activities. Overall, the evidence indicates that the JEC program increases educational attainment, with extended instructional time likely being one contributing factor among other improvements in school resources. JEC's effects on upward mobility, however, may remain limited without complementary measures that ease access to university education.

Title: Negotiating land, producing authority: hybrid rangeland governance on the pastoral Qinghai-Gansu Border, China
Abstract: Debates on property rights in pastoral China have largely focused on ownership, access, and more recently, transfer rights. However, everyday rangeland practices remain profoundly hybrid and insufficiently theorised. Drawing on eleven months of ethnographic fieldwork in Sog Zong, a pastoral county on the Qinghai-Gansu border, this paper examines how overlapping claims to rangeland are mediated through state contracts, religiously anchored agreements, village institutions, and conservation policies. Focusing on two cases, a bilateral rangeland use agreement historically mediated by the 10th Panchen Lama, and a recent state-led rangeland restoration project, the paper analyses how diverse institutional actors interact to shape access, exclusion, and control over land. Rather than treating these cases as instances of institutional plurality, the analysis demonstrates how authority is co-constituted across domains. The findings show that hybridity is best understood as a relational process in which authority emerges through ongoing practices of recognition, alignment, and contestation across institutional domains. This shifts analytical attention from identifying institutional diversity to examining how governance is actively produced through interaction. In doing so, the paper contributes to debates on hybrid governance and advances a practice-oriented understanding of property in pastoral contexts.

Title: The environmental smile curve: input-output evidence on the pollution haven hypothesis
Authors: Giovanni Dosi, Federico Riccio, Maria Enrica Virgillito
Abstract: This paper examines how the fragmentation of production across Global Value Chains (GVCs) generates both economic and environmental inequalities. Integrating OECD ICIO and CO 2 emission data, our analysis reveals an environmental smile curve, where environmental and economic downgrading co-occur in middle segments of GVCs, reinforcing global inequalities. These disparities intensify with deeper GVC penetration, challenging the decoupling narrative of green growth. By integrating labour and emission data, we provide novel evidence of how GVCs structurally embed asymmetric power relations between production segments, generating unequal ecological and economic burdens across the globe. While the Global North has strategically benefited from GVCs, the Global South has experienced the heightening of its peripheral and subordinated position.

Title: The impact of the Tigray war on child education and labor in Ethiopia
Abstract: This study provides the first empirical evidence on the impact of the Tigray War on children’s education and child labor in Ethiopia. We combine panel data from the 2018/19 and 2021/22 waves of the Ethiopian Socioeconomic Survey with geocoded conflict data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project. The analysis focuses on children aged 7–18 across Ethiopia, excluding Tigray due to data limitations and endogeneity concerns. We estimate a Difference-in-Differences model with child fixed effects to compare pre- and post-war outcomes based on proximity to conflict events. Results show that children near conflict zones were significantly less likely to attend school or plan future enrollment with effects concentrated among boys. Conflict exposure also increased child labor, particularly unpaid work for other households and state-led labor among boys. Further analysis and anecdotal evidence suggest that insecurity and state mobilization contributed to boys’ labor participation, ultimately disrupting their education.

Title: The two sides of migration in Central America: aggregate and distributional impacts in Guatemala
Authors: Luis Escalante, Emerta Aragie, Manuel A. Hernandez
Abstract: International migration affects labor supply, production patterns, and external income flows in origin countries, yet our understanding of its economy-wide and distributional consequences remains limited, particularly with regard to the role of return migration. This study integrates detailed microdata on migrant profiles into a general equilibrium model applied to Guatemala to examine how emigration and return migration affect macroeconomic performance, sectoral dynamics, and household welfare. We simulate three scenarios: a reference scenario reflecting recent-historical emigration patterns (MIG-0), a reduced-emigration scenario (MIG-1), and a net-return migration scenario (MIG-2), capturing recent shifts in emigration and return flows by skill level. Results reveal trade-offs between aggregate economic performance and distributional impacts across households. Compared to a baseline economy with no mobility, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rises modestly under the reference scenario (+0.2 percent) and by additional 0.3–0.5 percentage points under the reduced-emigration and net-return scenarios, driven by expanded labor supply from returnees and currency depreciation. Non-agro-processing manufacturing shows the largest expansion (up to 1.8 percent), reflecting its strong labor-absorption potential. Household welfare, especially among remittance-dependent households, is highly sensitive to these flows, with income and consumption declining under the two counterfactual migration scenarios. These findings underscore the need for policies that facilitate returnee reintegration and strengthen social protection for remittance-dependent households, ensuring that the macroeconomic gains from migration adjustments translate into equitable welfare improvements.

Title: No need to wait for reporting − Examining learning from results-based management practices in development cooperation
Authors: Janet Vähämäki, Annika Hilgert, Kathrin Wolf, Martin Bruder
Abstract: With today’s shrinking budgets for development cooperation and criticism that International Development Cooperation Organizations (IDOs) often fail to use performance data to inform decision-making, it is essential to know if and how IDOs learn from their results-based management (RBM) practices. Learning is typically assumed to happen in a cyclical RBM learning loop. Learning is supposed to occur in the final stage of the loop when reporting should inform future decisions. We propose a new heuristic model for learning and observe that learning from results is, in fact, taking place in IDOs, but not in the way previously envisaged. Drawing on qualitative semi-structured interviews with 15 IDOs, we conclude that learning takes place at earlier stages of the RBM cycle, and that the strongest link to learning is in the first stage of planning and forecasting. Moreover, we observe that artifacts, interactive and dynamic dialogue, and drawing on various knowledge sources are key characteristics of learning from results practices. Beyond these, we consider Theories of Change as an artifact to be more likely to enable learning than other artifacts like reports as they visualize how problems will be turned into desirable futures and often mobilize staff in interactive processes. These findings should inform efforts to improve future RBM models to enable learning from results in IDOs by putting more effort into using results information in decision-making, streamlining RBM processes, and providing additional support for processes during the first stage of the RBM loop.

Title: Long panel studies of small-scale rural societies in the Global South: What is their value, why are they rare, and suggestions to make them happen
Authors: Jonathan Bauchet, Ricardo Godoy, William R. Leonard, Victoria Reyes-García, Asher Y. Rosinger, Susan Tanner, Eduardo A. Undurraga
Abstract: Many topics in the behavioral sciences and epidemiology require researchers to directly observe entities (e.g., individuals, households) over a long time to identify lasting effects. Long-term panel data collection is more common in high-income countries than in small-scale rural societies (SSRS) of low-income countries. SSRS are mobile, nature-dependent, linguistic minorities, and highly autarkic. Analyzing such data using a life-course perspective can help uncover patterns that align or upend what we know from high-income countries. This study a) reviews long (>∼10 year) panels in SSRS (n = 9), b) extends the analysis to cover somewhat comparable societies of smallholders (n = 7) who are less autarkic, and c) draws on annual panel data (2002–2010) from one SSRS in the Bolivian Amazon (Tsimane’) to illustrate how adult life-course patterns may vary but also resemble patterns in high-income countries. In general, panels have focused more on human biology than on socioeconomic outcomes, have gathered data at irregular intervals, and have not deposited datasets in public repositories. Compared with people in high-income countries, Tsimane’ were similar in the amount of intragenerational immobility at the very top and the very bottom of the income and wealth distribution. In both places, body weight rose while sociality frayed over time. Yet Tsimane’ differed in having more economic mobility outside the top and bottom income and wealth distribution, a slightly higher growth rate in economic inequality, and no correlation between economic mobility and age. We identify institutional and individual hurdles to collecting panel data in SSRS and discuss steps to overcome them.

Title: FDI and coal lock-in: The Global South’s development dilemma
Authors: Xinya Hao, Lin Zhang, Huanhuan Zheng
Abstract: Why do poorer countries continue to adopt coal-fired power despite global climate pressures, while richer countries phase it out? This paper argues that the divergence in coal power phase-out trajectories between the Global North and South is driven by the coupling of greenfield investment with coal-fired power expansion in the Global South. Using matched global greenfield investments at the project level with coal plants at the city-level and employing the stacked DID strategy, we find that new coal-fired power installations increase cities’ inbound greenfield investment by 7.9% annually over eight years, particularly in low- and lower-middle-income countries; however, the inward capital is less oriented toward renewable technologies. This linkage arises from structural asymmetries: capital flows from the Global North to the South, the relocation of energy-intensive industries, and fragmented environmental regulation. Our findings highlight that the dilemma faced by developing countries: phasing out coal-fired power entails extremely high opportunity costs, while expanding coal power capacity crowds out investments in renewable technologies. Overall, we provide new evidence on how uneven development constraints result in fossil fuel dependency in the Global South.

Title: Unintended consequences of externally aided projects on fiscal transfers: a subnational study of India
Abstract: We investigate the impact of foreign aid on inter-governmental transfers in India. While anecdotal evidence suggests that the central government substitutes fiscal transfers with earmarked foreign aid for state governments (fungibility), empirical evidence is scant due to the complex procedure of accruing foreign aid by the states. By Constitutional design, all foreign aid projects procured by states accrue to the central government which are then distributed to states as Additional Central Assistance (ACA) on Externally Aided Projects (EAPs). Analysing panel data covering 29 states from 1979 to 2017, we find that EAPs per capita are positively associated with the central government fiscal transfers to states under discretionary head (resource loading), but not with formulaic transfers. Importantly, the positive effect of EAPs on discretionary transfers is contingent on political alignment between the central and state governments, a finding consistent with previous works that demonstrate how recipient governments target aid at the subnational level based on local political factors. These findings have significant policy implications for the centre, state governments, and external aid donors.

Title: Corporate governance in microfinance institutions: A systematic review of theoretical perspectives, methodological approaches, and empirical evidence
Authors: Giovanni Cardillo, Alessandra Cavallo, Giuseppe Torluccio
Abstract: Corporate governance in microfinance institutions (MFIs) significantly influences their ability to pursue financial sustainability and social outreach, yet two decades of empirical research have produced fragmented and contradictory findings. This paper presents a systematic review of 47 peer-reviewed studies published between 2005 and 2025 that examine how governance mechanisms shape MFI dual performance. Rather than treating theoretical concentration and empirical inconsistency as symptoms of weak scholarship, we demonstrate that both reflect structural constraints embedded in prevailing data infrastructures. Widely used datasets, most prominently MIX Market, disproportionately support agency-theoretic constructs while rendering relational, institutional, and stakeholder governance dimensions largely unobservable, systematically shaping theory selection, empirical strategy, and reported findings across the literature. Building on these considerations, the review makes three contributions. First, it provides a structural explanation for why agency theory dominates the field and argues that theoretical diversification requires investment in richer data rather than simply broader lens selection. Second, it demonstrates that standard governance variables function as bundled proxies whose effects are contingent on organizational form, regulatory status, and stakeholder structure, and proposes simultaneous equations modeling to capture the feedback loops between financial performance and social outreach that single-equation designs cannot estimate. Third, it identifies informal and relational governance mechanisms, trust-based networks, board members’ social capital, and stakeholder embeddedness as theoretically central but empirically absent, and proposes longitudinal and mixed-method designs to address this blind spot. Together, these contributions reframe the research agenda on MFI governance and call for a redefinition of effective governance in hybrid, mission-driven organizations.

Title: The mobilization curse? How oil wealth affects the composition of resistance episodes
Abstract: How does oil shape anti-state dissent? While previous research suggests that oil wealthy countries may be less likely to democratize and more likely to experience civil wars, few studies have examined how oil wealth shapes the broader composition of anti-state resistance, from political parties, to trade unions, and CSOs. We argue that high levels of oil wealth lower the probability that economically based organizations (such as trade unions) and civil society organizations participate in anti-state dissent by eroding the supply of these organizations and enabling selective cooptation and repression. However, we also argue that oil wealth does not impact political parties, armed rebel groups, and what we label “protest organizations” in the same way, leading to dissent that is more concentrated around organizations designed to capture state power. Using data on the organizational composition of resistance campaigns in Africa from 1990-2015, our findings suggest that high levels of oil wealth reduce the probability of observing economic organizations and CSOs among dissenting organizations and the probability that organizations in general mobilize from economic sectors. Mechanism tests suggest that oil limits the participation of economic organizations in dissent by shrinking or impeding the development of a strong manufacturing sector.

Title: Is there a business case for banks to increase lending to women and women-led firms? Cross-country evidence on financial performance
